chapter: Paris, the Blackbirds and Noble Sissle
title: Noble Sissle hires him at $300 a week
summary: Via violinist Andre Roseman, Sissle offered Briggs a post at the Ambassador and Ciro's, paying $300 weekly with responsibility for floor shows; he stresses playing quietly, unlike Guy Lombardo.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: And I stayed with them three months until Noble Sissle, still through the intermediary of Andro Roseman, who was with us as a violin player, with the Syncopated Orchestra, he was with Noble Sissle's Orchestra at the time, in London, and he wired me, saying Noble would like to contact me for his orchestra.
Well, seeing that I was going to have some difficulties in France on account of the labor permit, I did not know the conditions
Briggs
musicians well enough to choose what I wanted, so I just decided to disband, and go with Sissle, because Sissle paid me so much money.
So, in other words, Sissle had been conducting Lew Leslie's Blackbirds?
Yes -- no, no. No, Sissle's Orchestra was at the Ambassador.
Oh, I see, right.
And he had -- the Ambassador in Paris --
And he heard you play?
Yeh.
So he brought you to London then?
Yes. But before we went to London, we played the Ambassador about a year and a half, the Ambassador and Ciro's in Paris, you see. And Monte Carlo, 'cause you have a Ciro's in Monte Carlo.
Briggs 203
Apparently there was an agreement between Mr. Hobson who owns Ciro's clubs, the various Ciro's clubs, and Mr. Sayag, who was Managing Director of the Ambassador in Paris.
And all that was done through La Teague and Fisher's office, a booking office in Paris.
And I made my audition for Noble Sissle, and I got accepted, and he gave me, you wouldn't believe it, $300 a week.
Wow.
In those days -- but I had a lot of responsibility.
Right.
I had a lot of responsibilities, floor shows and everything I had to take over, you see.
But I was very, very satisfied with the work, -- say if you had four hours a day that was plenty. But we generally had two hours and a half, three hours.
Briggs
That's why I mentioned to you yesterday that you can give them what you want, play the way you want to, as long as it's not too noisy or boisterous.
Right.

And that was Sissle's work, and that's what we did, and we had the top work -- we were not conning. I don't want to criticize, but we were not Guy Lombardo, 'cause those guys are hard-headed, they wouldn't learn. They didn't try to ameliorate the situation. I imagine they still play the same way today.
Oh, sure. Sure, sure.
They're awful. I mean they have no feeling or nothing.
Yeh.
I guess it's just one of those things.
